accordions.heading: What is PSA?
accordions.content:
PSA (prostate-specific antigen) is a protein made by the prostate. It’s normal to have some PSA in your blood, and levels can increase as you get older.

Checking your PSA can help identify changes that may need further investigation. Raised levels can have several causes, including an enlarged prostate, inflammation or infection.

This home test checks whether your PSA level is around 4 ng/mL or higher. It doesn’t measure your exact PSA level.

accordions.heading: When to test
accordions.content:
Any time: You can take a PSA test at any time, but some activities and health conditions can affect your result.

Wait 48 hours: After ejaculation, anal sex, cycling or vigorous exercise.

Wait 4–6 weeks: After a urine infection has cleared.

If you’ve recently had a prostate procedure, ask your GP when it’s appropriate to test.

how.heading: How the PSA home test works
how.intro: This test uses a small finger-prick blood sample to check your PSA level. There’s no need to send anything to a lab, and you’ll get your result in around 15 minutes.

steps.title: Prick your finger
steps.text: Wash your hands, clean a fingertip with the alcohol pad and use the lancet to prick the side of it.

steps.title: Add blood and test liquid
steps.text: Using the pipette, add 3 drops of blood to the sample well, followed immediately by 1 drop of diluent (test liquid).

steps.title: Read at 15 minutes
steps.text: Leave the test pad flat. Read your result between 15 and 20 minutes. Do not read it after 20 minutes, as the result will be invalid.

groups.intro: Look at the result window. C is the control line and T is the test line. Compare how dark the lines are.

items.title: Negative — Below 4 ng/mL
items.text: One line appears at C, with no line at T, or two lines appear but the T line is lighter than C.

items.title: Positive — At or above 4 ng/mL
items.text: Two lines appear, and the T line is as dark as or darker than C.

items.title: Invalid — Test didn’t work
items.text: No line appears at C, even if a line appears at T.

notes.title: Good to know
notes.text: A raised PSA result doesn’t always mean you have a prostate problem, but it’s important to discuss it with your GP. A result below 4 ng/mL doesn’t rule out all prostate problems. See your GP if you have symptoms, such as needing to pee more often or difficulty peeing.

questions.question: Does this test tell me my exact PSA level?
questions.answer: No. This test checks whether your PSA level is around 4 ng/mL or higher. It doesn’t give you an exact number. A laboratory blood test can measure your PSA level more precisely.

questions.question: When should I test?
questions.answer:
Avoid ejaculation, anal sex, cycling and vigorous exercise for 48 hours before testing.

If you’ve had a urine infection, wait 4–6 weeks after it has cleared. If you’ve recently had a prostate procedure, ask your GP when to test.

questions.question: What if my result shows two lines?
questions.answer: Compare the T line with the C line. If the T line is lighter than C, your result is negative. If it’s as dark as or darker than C, your result is positive.

questions.question: What should I do if my result is positive?
questions.answer: Book an appointment with your GP to discuss your result. They may arrange another blood test to check your PSA level and advise you on the next steps.

questions.question: Does a negative result mean my prostate is healthy?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. A result below 4 ng/mL doesn’t rule out all prostate problems. If you have symptoms or concerns, speak to your GP.

questions.question: What can raise my PSA?
questions.answer: PSA levels can rise for several reasons, including an enlarged prostate, an infection, inflammation or recent exercise. A raised level can also be a sign of prostate cancer, but it doesn’t necessarily mean you have cancer.
